title: Kim v. Korean Eastern Presbytery
disposition_detail: The SJC sustained the contumacy judgment; sustained deposition but replaced excommunication with indefinite suspension from the sacraments; and did not sustain the civil-lawsuit-threat judgment.
first_summary: A minister appealed his convictions for contumacy and threatening elders with civil litigation, together with deposition and excommunication. The SJC sustained the contumacy conviction and deposition, but deemed excommunication excessive and replaced it with indefinite suspension from the sacraments. It did not sustain the threat conviction because the attorney’s letter underlying that charge was absent from the record and therefore could not constitutionally be considered.
summary: A minister appealed convictions for contumacy and threatening elders with civil litigation, plus deposition and excommunication. The SJC sustained contumacy as failure to remain subject to the brethren under the ordination vow, not BCO 32-6-type contumacy. It sustained deposition but found excommunication excessive given the conflict and replaced it with indefinite suspension from the sacraments. It did not sustain the threat conviction because the attorney’s letter was absent from the record. A dissent disputed the contumacy ruling.

evidence_notes.identity_and_adoption: The heading identifies Case 2005-8 as Kim’s appeal against Korean Eastern Presbytery; the SJC adopted the decision 17-1 (printed pp. 131, 133; lines 13, 54–62).
evidence_notes.dispute: Kim appealed the contumacy and lawsuit-threat judgments and the censures of deposition and excommunication (printed pp. 131–132; lines 17–41).
evidence_notes.outcomes_and_reasons: Contumacy and deposition were sustained; excommunication was changed to indefinite sacramental suspension as excessive; the threat judgment failed because its letter was absent from the record (printed p. 132; lines 35–52).
evidence_notes.qualifications: The majority distinguished the sustained contumacy from BCO 32-6 contumacy. The lower court’s acquittal on the property charge was not an appellate issue. The contrary discussion beginning at line 64 is a dissent (printed pp. 131–138; lines 19, 25–52, 64–256).
